title: the dice game
hook: Duryodhana and Shakuni work on the blind king, a hall is built for the game, and Vidura's warning goes unheeded
carry: let a worry change one thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road home, Duryodhana spoke his envy aloud, and Shakuni offered a plan to win without a war. Name the sting before it becomes a plan.

A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura. So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong. The plan moves from a road to a throne room, and a father has to decide.
screen: `A PLAN NEEDS PERMISSION.` → `TO THE BLIND KING.` → `A FATHER ASKS WHAT'S WRONG.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni: the Pandavas' wealth, the kings at their feet, the hall that shamed him. And Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother, whose counsel he trusts. Duryodhana pushes back hard, in effect: ask Vidura, and Vidura will stop it, and I'll be lost. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a splendid new hall built for the game, worthy of the guests. Only then does he call Vidura, not to ask whether, but to tell him. Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve. This game, he warns, will set the cousins against each other and end in quarrel. Dhritarashtra doesn't change course. If the gods are kind, he answers, no harm will come; what is fated will happen. Then he gives Vidura a job: go to Indraprastha, and bring Yudhishthira here to play. Look at that. The one man who sees the danger clearly is sent to deliver the invitation. A father who couldn't say no to his son has made the counselor he trusts most the messenger of the thing he warned against. The poem doesn't call Dhritarashtra wicked. It shows a man who heard the warning, and loved his son too much to act on it.
screen: `DHRITARASHTRA HESITATES.` · `DURYODHANA PUSHES PAST VIDURA.` · `A HALL IS BUILT FOR THE GAME.` · `VIDURA WARNS, AND IS SENT ANYWAY.` · then, large: `HE HEARD THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you said yes to someone you love when part of you wanted to say no, and picture the moment you gave way. There's no grade here; just notice what made the yes easier, and whether a no might have been a kind of care too. If you pray, you can bring that yes, and that person, to your prayer; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Vidura. The counselor who warns that this game will end in quarrel, and is sent anyway, by the father who couldn't refuse his son, to carry the invitation he spoke against.
Your line: let a worry change one thing. Dhritarashtra heard Vidura, and changed nothing. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

original.note: Sanskrit vidura: the name of Dhritarashtra's half-brother, the counselor who warns against the game.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dice game was the Pandavas' choice.
what it means: it was set up in Hastinapura, approved by a father who couldn't refuse his son, against Vidura's warning.
what a scholar hears: Dhritarashtra answers a clear warning by appealing to fate, which lets him go ahead without owning the choice.
recall: the boat waiting at the Ganga

chat.says: If Vidura warned the king about the game, why did he deliver the invitation?
options: The king heard his warning but sent him anyway, unable to refuse his son.
Vidura changed his mind once he saw the splendid new hall being built.
Vidura wanted the game so the Pandavas could win back their honor.
chat.meaning: Vidura said the game would end in quarrel. Dhritarashtra, who couldn't say no to Duryodhana, made him the messenger anyway.

Dhritarashtra.meaning: the blind king of Hastinapura, Duryodhana's father

Vidura.meaning: the blind king's half-brother and wise counselor

Hastinapura.meaning: the Kuru capital, home of Duryodhana and his brothers

Indraprastha.meaning: the Pandavas' city, where the Rajasuya is held

Shakuni.meaning: Duryodhana's uncle, a master at dice

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Shakuni and Duryodhana persuade Dhritarashtra; the hall built; Vidura's warning; Vidura sent to invite Yudhishthira)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Shakuni speaks of Duryodhana's pallor; Dhritarashtra wishes to consult Vidura first; Duryodhana objects that Vidura will dissuade him (Ganguli also has him threaten his own life; omitted here).
Confirm the order: the hall is ordered built before Vidura is told, and Vidura's warning is about dissension among the sons.
Confirm Dhritarashtra's reply appeals to the gods and to fate, and that he sends Vidura to Indraprastha to invite Yudhishthira.
Trapdoor third floor: 'a move the poem returns to at many hard turns' is a general claim about the poem; a Keeper may soften or cut.
The game itself and Yudhishthira's response to the invitation are left for day 767.
